title: Complete layer feed
body: Use a complete feed labelled for adult laying hens. A useful planning baseline is about 115 g per hen daily; real intake varies with breed, temperature and production. Follow the feed label and monitor body condition. Do not give high-calcium layer feed to growing chicks. Keep fresh water available.

title: Everyday biosecurity
body: Keep wild birds and rodents away from feed and water. Use dedicated coop footwear and wash hands after handling birds or equipment. Keep new arrivals separate and ask a veterinarian about a suitable quarantine plan. Clean drinkers and keep bedding dry. Avoid sharing equipment between flocks.

title: Respiratory warning signs
body: Wheezing, repeated sneezing, discharge, reduced appetite or unusual quietness need attention. Separate an unwell bird, provide water and contact a poultry veterinarian. Breathing difficulty or sudden deaths require urgent advice. A journal cannot identify the cause; do not choose medicines from symptoms alone.

title: Mites and parasites
body: Check feather bases, skin and coop crevices for irritation or tiny moving specks. Pale combs, feather damage and reduced laying can have many causes. Record what you see and ask a poultry veterinarian to identify the problem before treatment. Keep bedding clean and inspect the rest of the flock.

title: Changes in laying
body: Age, moulting, daylight, stress and nutrition can change egg numbers. Compare daily records over several weeks rather than assuming disease from one low day. Straining, weakness or a swollen abdomen need prompt veterinary assessment. Do not attempt to remove an egg yourself.

title: Sudden illness in the flock
body: Sudden deaths, severe breathing trouble or several sick birds at once need urgent veterinary advice. Keep people and equipment from moving between flocks. Contact your local animal-health authority about current avian influenza guidance and reporting rules. The offline guide does not provide current outbreak status.
